messages.subject: The Hashmat class
parts:
Hi Kylie,

I am currently using Cardinal version 1.6.0, and I have noticed that you have implemented a new class for storing the sparse spectral signals using the Hashmat class. Previously, I was able to convert the spectral data into a simple R matrix using "spectra(object)" or "iData(object)", however, this is no longer possible since using the "spectra()" method produces a Hashmat object and applying "pData()" on that produces a list of spectra whose elements are its non-zero elements i.e. they have different lengths. Is there still a simple way to convert the spectral content of an MSImageSet object into a simple R matrix? 

Thanks,
Denis

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: The Hashmat class
parts:
Hi Denis,

Hashmat has been around since v1.0, so there hasn't been a change. Are your datasets the "processed" version of imzML? For that format (only), Cardinal must default to using Hashmat rather than an ordinary R matrix, due to the differences in how its stored vs. "continuous" imzML.

In any case, yes. You can simply do "spectra(object)[,]" or "iData(object)[,]". (The comma is actually optional as well.) Subsetting without indices will extract the full dense matrix as an R matrix. Depending on the size of the dataset, it may take some time to construct the dense matrix.

-Kylie

Hi all,

I wrote a work-around for writing continuous imzMLs from Cardinal using MALDIquant. However, MALDIquant does not store any experiment metadata besides imaging resolution (for now), but it may help in any case. I haven't tested it with other softwares at all.

This just makes a list of MALDIquant MassSpectrum objects from the iData and mz of a Cardinal dataset which can be written into an imzML. I think you could make it to work with processed data with a few tweaks. This will work with peak picked data as well as full range mass data, but beware of memory problems if writing full range data (not sure how it will work if loading off hard disk either). If using peak picked data, other softwares will likely assume the data is full range data and you'll have ugly specs in display, but the peak data should still be good.


##install and load required packages

install.packages("MALDIquant")
install.packages("MALDIquantForeign")
require(MALDIquant)
require(MALDIquantForeign)

cardinaldata <- DAN_001.peaks

#function for writing continuous imzML from continous Cardinal data

writeImzML <- function(cardinaldata, filepath = "myimzML.imzML", processed = FALSE, pixelSize= c(100, 100)){
  
  #matrix of integer coordinates
  xy <- as.matrix(Cardinal::coord(cardinaldata)[,1:2])
  
  #mz axis of continuous dataset
  mzs <- Cardinal::mz(cardinaldata)

  #initialize list for storage of spectra
  mq <- list()
  
  #loop through each column of the cardinal iData and create MALDIquant objects
  for(i in 1:ncol(cardinaldata)){
    mq[[i]] <- createMassSpectrum(mass = mzs, intensity = iData(cardinaldata)[,i])
  }
  
  #write using MALDIquantForeign's routine
  exportImzMl(mq, path = filepath, force = TRUE, processed = processed,
              coordinates = xy, pixelSize = pixelSize)
  
}


Heath
